LONDON, England (CNN) -- British TV channels could advertise abortion services for the first time under new advertising rules proposed Thursday by an ad industry group. The new proposals will also allow condoms to be advertised more widely on television. The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice, the industry body responsible for writing and enforcing advertising rules in Britain, said the commercials would be for pregnancy advisory services that give information about a range of options to pregnant women, including abortion. If an organization does not offer information about abortion, it would have to make that clear in the ad, BCAP spokeswoman Lynsay Taffe said. Abortion clinics, which require referrals from doctors or hospitals, would not be allowed to advertise under the proposed rules, Taffe said. There would be no restrictions on when such ads could air on British television, she said, but programmers would have to keep the sensitive topic in mind and not schedule the ads around religious programs, for example. "It's a sensitive product, so it would have to be scheduled sensitively," Taffe told CNN. The proposal is among a number of updates to current advertising standards that the Committee for Advertising Practice and BCAP, its broadcasting arm, published Thursday after an 18-month review. "Each year the British public (sees) millions of advertisements, many of which are memorable," the committee said. "The advertising codes aim to make sure that they are memorable for the right reasons." The public now has until June 19 to comment on the proposals before they come into force, likely in 2010, the committee said. The new proposals also contain a change on advertising condoms on television. Under current rules, condoms generally cannot be advertised on TV before 9 p.m. in order to protect younger viewers, the committee said. New rules would relax the restrictions on advertising condoms, with the only requirement that they not be shown around programs intended for children younger than 10. The change came after Joyce Gould, a member of the House of Lords, requested the change and noted that Britain had the highest teenage pregnancy rate in Europe along with spiraling rates of sexually transmitted diseases, the committee said. Gould reported a survey that showed young people believed TV was one of the most effective ways of encouraging them to use condoms. "The presence of condom advertisements on television continues to be a subject of complaint to the (Advertising Standards Authority), but numbers are very low," the committee said. "Nevertheless, BCAP has to balance public sensitivities against a public health problem that is clearly urgent."

**UK Proposes Landmark Overhaul of TV Advertising Rules for Abortion Services and Condoms**

In a major move toward modernizing public health broadcasting, Britain’s advertising regulator has unveiled proposals to lift longstanding bans and restrictions on television commercials for pregnancy advisory services and condoms. The proposed changes, published for public comment by the Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice (BCAP), follow a comprehensive 18-month review aimed at bringing outdated regulatory standards in line with contemporary societal attitudes and public health needs.

If adopted, the revised guidelines would represent a historic shift in British media policy. For the first time in history, post-conception pregnancy advisory services—including organizations that provide advice on and referrals for abortion—would be permitted to advertise on television. Concurrently, the strict time restrictions that currently dictate when condom advertisements can be aired would be dismantled, allowing them to appear during daytime broadcasting hours.

### Modernizing Outdated Standards

The regulatory overhaul comes in response to growing recognition that Britain’s existing broadcast advertising code no longer reflects modern realities. For decades, regulations surrounding sexual and reproductive health were governed by strict rules designed to shield viewers from topics deemed sensitive or taboo. However, public health advocates and broadcasters have increasingly argued that these restrictions hinder access to crucial information, disproportionately affecting vulnerable individuals facing unplanned pregnancies or seeking guidance on sexual health.

BCAP’s 18-month review carefully evaluated public attitudes, broadcaster concerns, and health sector recommendations. The committee concluded that television remains a vital, trusted medium for delivering essential health messaging, and that restrictive policies were actively insulating the public from vital support services.

### Access to Pregnancy Advice and Abortion Services

Under the current framework, television advertising for post-conception services—specifically those offering guidance on abortion—is entirely banned. The new proposal would allow impartial, non-profit, and statutory pregnancy advisory clinics to advertise, provided their messages adhere to strict standards of accuracy and responsibility.

Health organizations and family planning groups have widely welcomed the move, emphasizing that early access to impartial information is critical for women making time-sensitive decisions about unplanned pregnancies. Proponents argue that allowing these services to air on television will help destigmatize reproductive healthcare, reduce misinformation, and ensure that women know where to seek confidential, professional help.

To address potential concerns, BCAP’s proposed framework includes safeguards to ensure that advertisements remain informative and sensitive, preventing misleading claims or overly sensationalized content.

### Normalizing Condom Advertising

The proposed rules also target restrictions on condom commercials, which have historically been subject to rigid scheduling limits, often restricted to late-night viewing hours well past the traditional 9:00 PM "watershed." 

Under the new draft code, these artificial time barriers would be removed, allowing condom manufacturers to advertise throughout the day, provided the creative content of the ad is suitable for general audiences. Regulators believe this change will help normalize conversations around safe sex, contribute to the reduction of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and decrease rates of unintended teenage pregnancies.

### Public Consultation and Next Steps

The publication of these proposed rules marks the beginning of a formal public consultation period, during which BCAP is inviting feedback from viewers, healthcare professionals, religious institutions, and broadcasting stakeholders. 

While the proposals have drawn praise from public health advocates and media outlets, they are expected to spark debate among socially conservative groups and anti-abortion organizations, who argue that daytime broadcasts of such topics may be inappropriate for younger audiences.

BCAP maintains that the consultation process will ensure a balanced final decision, weighing public interest and health education against the need to protect viewers from unsuitable content. If approved following the consultation, the new code will mark a landmark milestone in British broadcasting history, reframing reproductive health not as a subject for censorship, but as a critical component of public well-being.

**LONDON** — British television viewers could soon see condom advertisements aired during daytime television and the first-ever TV commercials for abortion services, under major regulatory changes proposed by the UK’s advertising watchdog.

The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice (BCAP), which sets the codes for TV and radio commercials, has launched a public consultation on relaxing longstanding restrictions on sexual health and pregnancy advice advertising. 

The proposed reforms aim to bring broadcast advertising into line with modern public health priorities, specifically targeting rising rates of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) among young people and high rates of unintended teenage pregnancies.

### **Ending the 9pm Watershed Ban on Condoms**

Under current rules, advertisements for condoms and contraception are strictly restricted to late-night slots, generally prohibited before the 9:00 pm watershed to protect younger viewers from adult themes. 

Under the new proposals, condom manufacturers would be permitted to advertise at any time of day, provided the content of the commercial is responsibly scheduled and appropriate for a general audience. 

Health campaigners have long argued that the watershed restriction sends a harmful message that condom use is taboo, rather than a routine component of safe sex and public health education. 

### **A Historic Shift on Abortion Services**

In what would mark a historic shift in British broadcasting, the proposals also seek to end the outright ban on television and radio advertising for post-conception advice services, including organizations that offer lawful abortion procedures.

Historically, advertising for pregnancy advice services that included abortion options was prohibited under rules governing contentious medical procedures and moral issues. Under the new draft rules, non-profit healthcare providers and charities—such as Marie Stopes International and the British Pregnancy Advisory Service (BPAS)—would be allowed to advertise their services, including free advisory helplines and abortion care.

The proposed code specifies that any such advertisements must remain strictly informational, non-judgmental, and focused on offering confidential advice and support, rather than promoting abortion as a commercial product.

### **Fierce Debate Over Proposals**

The announcement has ignited a sharp debate between sexual health advocates and traditionalist and pro-life campaign groups.

Sexual health charities and medical bodies have strongly welcomed the move. Representatives from the Family Planning Association (FPA) argued that the media plays a vital role in normalizing sexual health and ensuring women know where to access unbiased advice in a crisis. 

"At a time when teenage pregnancy rates in the UK remain among the highest in Western Europe, restricting vital information to late midnight slots is out of touch," said a spokesperson for sexual health advocates. "Women need clear, rapid access to impartial advice."

However, the proposals have drawn heavy criticism from pro-life organizations and media watchdog groups.

The Society for the Protection of Unborn Children (SPUC) condemned the plan to allow abortion services on television, warning it would "commercially promote" a sensitive and morally contentious procedure. 

Meanwhile, family values campaign group Mediawatch-UK expressed concern over the relaxation of condom advertising rules, arguing that daytime commercials would expose young children to sexualized concepts before they are emotionally ready, undermining parental control.

### **Next Steps**

The BCAP consultation will run for several months to gather feedback from the public, broadcasters, health professionals, and special interest groups. 

If approved by the main regulator, Ofcom, the revised rules are expected to come into effect later next year, paving the way for the first pregnancy advice commercials featuring abortion options to appear on commercial channels such as ITV, Channel 4, and Five.

**BREAKING THE TABOO: HOW RELAXING BROADCAST AD CODES HELPED REFRAME UK PUBLIC HEALTH AND SLASH TEEN PREGNANCY RATES**

**LONDON** — For decades, the United Kingdom held an unwelcome title: the teenage pregnancy capital of Western Europe. In the late 1990s, nearly 50 out of every 1,000 young women aged 15 to 17 became pregnant each year—a statistic that fueled intense political debate, strained public services, and prompted decades of social soul-searching.

While sex education in schools and improved community healthcare clinic access were long seen as the primary battlegrounds, an equally critical—and fierce—fight took place in the control rooms of the nation’s media regulators. 

A pivotal chapter in the UK's public health strategy relied on a pragmatic overhaul of broadcast advertising rules. By modernizing codes governing the television and radio promotion of condoms and pregnancy advisory services, regulators transformed the airwaves from spaces of enforced silence into vital conduits for public health messaging.

### The "Moral Hazard" Era: The Watershed Wall

Prior to major regulatory interventions, broadcast advertising for sexual health products was strictly constrained by morality codes dating back to the mid-20th century. Under the Independent Television Authority and later the Radio Authority, advertisements for condoms were largely restricted to late-night slots well past the 9:00 PM "watershed"—the time when media content was deemed suitable for children to watch or hear. 

Worse still, advertisements for pregnancy advice services—particularly those offering impartial information on abortion—were effectively banned from television and radio under strict rules preventing commercial broadcasts from touching on "morally sensitive issues."

Public health advocates argued that these restrictions created a dangerous paradox. While television programming increasingly reflected youth culture and sexual themes, the commercial breaks were legally barred from providing the basic tools and advice needed for safe, informed choices.

"The old ad codes effectively treated safe sex and reproductive healthcare as shameful secrets," says Dr. Helen Finch, a public health historian. "Young people were bombarded with sexualized media, but the broadcast rules prevented health organizations from meeting them where they were—on daytime TV and mainstream radio."

### The Regulatory Overhaul: BCAP and Ofcom Step In

The turning point began following the launch of the government’s landmark 1999 *Teenage Pregnancy Strategy*, a 10-year action plan aimed at halving under-18 conception rates. Recognizing that public awareness was a core pillar of the strategy, public health officials joined forces with media regulators to modernize the rules.

The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice (BCAP)—the body responsible for writing the UK Code of Broadcast Advertising, enforced by the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) and overseen by Ofcom—initiated a series of radical updates.

The proposed and eventually adopted updates focused on three core areas:

1. **Scheduling Flexibility for Condoms:** BCAP relaxed the blanket post-watershed restriction on condom advertisements. Regulators allowed ads to air earlier in the evening and during daytime programming, provided the content was not scheduled around programs aimed directly at children. The messaging shifted from purely disease prevention (a legacy of the 1980s HIV/AIDS campaigns) to promoting responsible, everyday protection.
2. **Access for Pregnancy Advisory Services:** In one of the most contentious policy shifts, regulators updated the codes to permit non-profit and independent pregnancy advisory services to advertise on television and radio. This allowed organizations such as the British Pregnancy Advisory Service (BPAS) and Marie Stopes UK (now MSI Reproductive Choices) to broadcast information regarding pregnancy testing, unbiased counseling, and post-conception options, including abortion.
3. **Tone and Responsibility Mandates:** To balance public health imperatives with viewer sensibilities, the new codes established strict qualitative guidelines. Advertisements were required to be non-sensational, factually accurate, and presented with a high degree of social responsibility, ensuring they did not encourage premature sexual activity or cause undue offense.

### Backlash and the Public Debate

The proposals sparked immediate controversy from social conservative groups, church organizations, and traditionalist media watchdogs. Opponents argued that bringing condom and pregnancy advice ads into daytime broadcasting would "normalize" underage sexual activity and bypass parental authority.

During public consultations on the code revisions, critics warned that television screens would be flooded with inappropriate content. Questions were raised in Parliament over whether state-sanctioned media was undermining family values, with traditionalist groups mounting legal and public pressure campaigns to block pregnancy advisory ads, particularly those referencing abortion.

However, public health groups, backed by statistical evidence, successfully argued that silence carried a far higher social and financial cost.

"The opposition was rooted in fear, but the policy was rooted in data," says Sharon White, a former youth sexual health advocate involved in the consultations during the mid-2000s. "Hiding information didn't stop teenagers from having sex; it just stopped them from using contraception or seeking early advice when things went wrong. Normalizing these conversations on television was essential to removing the stigma."

### The Results: A Public Health Success Story

The integration of modernized broadcast advertising into the broader health strategy yielded dramatic, historic results.

By 2021, the under-18 conception rate in England and Wales had fallen by over 60% compared to its 1998 peak—reaching the lowest levels since records began in 1969. While experts attribute this success to a combination of factors, including improved sex education, better access to long-acting reversible contraception (LARC), and shifting youth cultural habits, the role of broadcast media in changing social norms is widely acknowledged as a catalyst.

By treating condoms and pregnancy advice as routine health topics rather than taboo adult content, the updated ad codes helped demystify contraception for a generation of young people. 

### A Model for the Digital Age

Today, the battleground for health information has largely shifted from linear television to social media platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube. Yet, the lessons learned from the UK’s overhaul of broadcast advertising codes remain highly relevant.

Regulators worldwide now look to the UK’s experience as a case study in how media regulation can align with public health priorities without compromising public standards.

By treating the broadcast screen not as a moral battleground, but as a public health tool, the UK proved that changing the rules of what can be said—and when—can alter the course of a nation’s health trajectory.

Regulators say the overhaul reflects a growing consensus that commercial media should play a role in promoting public health and informed choice, rather than treating sexual health as a broadcast taboo.

"Advertising standards must reflect the values and needs of modern society," a spokesperson for BCAP said in a statement accompanying the decision. "Removing unnecessary restrictions on pregnancy advice and easing scheduling rules for contraception allows broadcasters to air vital public health information without compromising viewer protection."

Under the updated guidelines, pregnancy advisory services will be permitted to advertise, provided the spots remain impartial, non-judgmental, and clear about the range of options offered—including keeping the baby, adoption, and pregnancy termination. 

For condom manufacturers, the decision eases scheduling bottlenecks, allowing brands to air ads during daytime and early evening slots, provided the content remains tactful and appropriate for general audiences.

### Health charities welcome the move

The regulatory shift has drawn praise from public health organizations, sexual health charities, and family planning advocates across the UK, who have long argued that restrictive advertising rules hindered efforts to reduce unplanned pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections (STIs).

"For years, strict ad rules treated sexual health like something to be ashamed of or hidden after dark," said Richard Sherwood, a policy director at a London-based sexual health advocacy group. "By allowing condom ads during mainstream viewing hours and opening the door for pregnancy advice, regulators are helping to destigmatize basic healthcare. Information is empowerment."

Health experts note that younger demographics, who are most at risk for STIs and unplanned pregnancies, are increasingly exposed to unverified health claims online. Bringing regulated, factual advice to television is seen as a way to counterbalance digital misinformation.

### Balancing sensitivity and prime-time TV

While the move has been broadly welcomed by health advocates, the changes have sparked some debate among family values groups, who express concern about sensitive topics being broadcast during times when young children are likely watching.

Regulators have sought to reassure the public that strict content guidelines will remain in place. Commercials will still be vetted by Clearcast—the body that approves ads before they air—to ensure they do not feature overly explicit imagery or language inappropriate for family viewing.

"This is not a free-for-all," BCAP emphasized. "The tone of these advertisements must remain responsible, sensitive, and contextually appropriate."

### A modernizing media landscape

The UK’s move mirrors a broader trend across Europe, where regulators are increasingly viewing advertising rules through the lens of harm reduction and public education rather than traditional moral gatekeeping. 

For British broadcasters, the policy shift opens up new commercial opportunities while placing the UK’s TV regulations in line with digital platforms, where health messaging has operated with far fewer restrictions for years. 

The new advertising rules are expected to take effect immediately, with the first wave of updated pregnancy advisory and contraceptive campaigns set to hit British screens in the coming weeks.
